pages.text: Every morning, the road to Palmview Basic School smelled of waakye, fried plantain, kenkey and fried fish. Food sellers lined both sides, and hundreds of workers, students and travellers bought their breakfast. Madam Mills, the waakye seller, had fed the road for twenty years. “This pot pays school fees for my three children,” she often said. Nobody on the road doubted that she worked hard.

“This pot pays school fees for my three children,” she often said.
Nobody on the road doubted that she worked hard.
pages.alt: A busy road lined with food sellers, steaming pots and customers at breakfast time.

pages.text: But the road had a problem. After breakfast, the gutters beside it were clogged with leaves, plastic bags and greasy water. When it rained, the water spilled over onto the road and into the shops. Jonathan, the SRC prefect, and his classmate Rahinatu photographed it. “It smells,” said Rahinatu. “And the mosquitoes breed there.” Jonathan wrote in his notebook: Effect one, choked gutters.

pages.text: Then there was the traffic. Stalls spread onto the pavements, so students had to walk in the road. One afternoon, a motorbike skidded and nearly hit a girl in Class 1. “That could have been a tragedy,” said Rahinatu. Jonathan underlined: Effect two, crowded pavements and danger to pedestrians. “We must tell the Assembly,” he said. “But we must be fair to the sellers too.”

pages.text: Jonathan went to talk to Madam Mills. She listened carefully. “I do not want children hurt,” she said. “But where would we go? Without this road, there is no income for my family.” She showed him her bin, which she emptied every evening, and said that some sellers did the same. “Not everyone does,” she admitted. “The road needs a plan, not a ban.”

pages.text: Jonathan met Mr Zormelo, an environmental officer. “A proper food court near the school, with bins, running water, covered drains and a licence for each seller, would solve both problems,” said Mr Zormelo. “It must be built with the sellers, not against them.” Jonathan wrote: Solution, a designated food court. “Now,” he said, “I know exactly what to write in my letter.”

pages.text: Jonathan put his address at the top right, SRC Office, Palmview Basic School, Box 40, Kumasi, and below it the date, 14th June, 2027. On the left he wrote: The Municipal Chief Executive, Greater Okuapa Municipal Assembly, Box 1, Kumasi. “Dear Sir,” he began, and the heading read: THE EFFECTS OF STREET FOOD VENDING ON OUR COMMUNITY AND A SOLUTION. His first paragraph read: “I am writing on behalf of the pupils of Palmview Basic School to bring to your attention two problems caused by food selling along our road, and to propose a solution. We respect the sellers, who feed our community and support their families.”

pages.alt: A boy writes the first part of a formal letter with his address, the date and the receiver’s title at the top.

pages.text: He continued: “First, the gutters are choked with plastic and greasy water. As a result, rainwater floods the road, and mosquitoes breed in the standing water, which may spread malaria. Second, stalls cover the pavements, so pupils must walk in the road. Consequently, a pupil was nearly knocked down last week. To solve both problems, I suggest a designated food court near the school with bins, covered drains, running water and licences for all sellers, planned together with the sellers. This will protect health, keep the road safe and protect their income. I shall be grateful for your kind consideration. Yours faithfully, Jonathan Gyimah, SRC Prefect.” He signed above his full name.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: this letter has the writer’s address, the date, the recipient’s designation and full address, “Dear Sir”, a heading, “Yours faithfully”, a signature and the writer’s full name. It has two effects and one solution, each in its own paragraph, linked with “First”, “Second”, “As a result” and “Consequently”. It is polite, clear and persuasive, with no contractions or slang. Jonathan was fair to the sellers, and fairness persuades. The end.
